Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> National Abu Jinapor accuses Mahama gov’t of double standards over presidential jet purchase Source : Prince Adu-Owusu 17 November 2026 8:49pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
The Ranking Member of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs and Regional Integration Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, has accused the Mahama administration of double standards over its decision to purchase a new presidential jet, citing previous criticisms by the President and Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa of similar acquisitions.
He said the National Democratic Congress, while in opposition, defended the condition of the existing presidential aircraft and criticised proposals to acquire a new one, arguing that spending taxpayers' money on luxurious presidential jets was insensitive.
Speaking on JoyNews’ The Pulse on Tuesday, November 17, Mr Jinapor said the party had previously maintained that the Falcon aircraft acquired under former President John Agyekum Kufuor was in good condition and fit for purpose.
He cited a statement made by President Mahama, then a presidential candidate, in which he described spending taxpayers' money on luxurious jets as an act of unpardonable disrespect and insensitivity.
'Here we are, myjoyonline report, and I can hand it over to you, where President Mahama himself, then presidential candidate, states, and I quote, spending taxpayers' money on luxurious jets, quote, is unpardonable disrespect and insensitive.
"And it goes on and on and on, how President Mahama was making the point that it is not prudent to spend money to purchase a presidential jet or to spend money for the President's travels when it comes to a presidential jet," he said.
Mr Jinapor also referred to comments made by Mr Ablakwa on November 10, 2021, when he was a Ranking Member of Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee.
According to him, the Minister had cited the use of ageing presidential aircraft by other countries to argue that Ghana's existing Falcon was not too old to serve its purpose.
He said Mr Ablakwa had pointed to Namibia's use of a 30-year-old presidential jet, the 31-year-old aircraft used by then US President Joe Biden, and the French President's continued use of a presidential jet commissioned in 2010, the same year as Ghana's aircraft.
"Not too long after, we have been told that somehow the Falcon is not fit for purpose, maintaining is so difficult, and so on and so forth. And you see the minority, and I quote, minority will reject any move by government to purchase a new presidential jet," Mr Jinapor said.
He further questioned the government's justification for spending GH¢720 million on the new Falcon 6X at a time when many Ghanaians were facing economic difficulties.
The former Lands and Natural Resources Minister cited the financial challenges confronting judicial service workers, teachers and nurses, including concerns over their conditions of service and allowances.
He also pointed to unemployment among the youth and rising living costs, arguing that public resources should instead be directed towards productive sectors capable of stimulating economic growth and creating jobs.
Mr Jinapor questioned the government's claim that the country's economic conditions justified the purchase, particularly when workers in various sectors were demanding better conditions of service.
"The Minister is telling us that, in fact, the money that was approved by Parliament, the money that has been programmed to purchase two jets and four helicopters, is 1.2 billion United States dollars. If you convert it to Ghana cedis, it's 14 billion Ghana cedis. The Minister is telling us that the economic conditions of Ghana are so good.
"... Today, he says economic conditions are so good, and therefore, I think you should have found a different justification for this purchase of a presidential jet, and therefore, we are entitled as a country to spend 720 million Ghana cedis, and if you stretch it in terms of the plan that the government has, 14 billion Ghana cedis, ultimately, to purchase a presidential jet for the use of the president.”
